events.title: A lot needs an appraisal before a promise is made

variants.text:
The goods have a noticeable feature, but its origin is unclear. You record what is known, which checks are still needed, and where the appraisal remains an inference instead of presenting confidence as expertise.

The first appraisal does not fit the package condition or the supplier notes. You make a second check and preserve the discrepancy in the record so the decision rests on observation rather than a desired result.

If the scale reading does not explain an unusual property of the goods, you preserve that uncertainty in the record. The tool helps expose a discrepancy rather than turning incomplete data into a confident answer.

Arcana helps when unusual goods have a noticeable but incompletely understood property. A competent appraisal may end with an honest 'not yet known' and does not become a universal way to discover price.

choices.label: Apply the Arcana uncertainty method
choices.text: Use the published Merchant-local School fact to record what is known and what remains uncertain; it does not set a price.

choices.label: Use the appraisal scales
choices.text: Compare the lot with a concrete Merchant tool; the result improves evidence quality, not a universal price formula.

choices.label: Compare condition and notes
choices.text: Record what can be observed and keep uncertainty explicit.

choices.label: Decline a confident valuation
choices.text: Refuse to pretend certainty; ordinary trade remains available.

events.title: A trade needs terms that can be checked later

variants.text:
The seal on the manifest looks familiar, but one line does not match the actual cargo. You pause confirmation, compare the copies, and ask for the record to be corrected before handing the goods over.

The record shows a profit after the trade completes, but the next delivery requires costs before payment arrives. You distinguish final gain from funds available now without creating a separate finance system.

Formal wording can sound impressive while still obscuring who is responsible for what. You restate the term in plain language and check that both sides understand the obligation the same way.

It helps to keep a short plain-language explanation beside a complicated manifest term. The case keeps both versions together so a formal document does not become a convenient place for ambiguity.

choices.label: Verify against the manifest case
choices.text: Use the prepared manifest tool to compare terms and cargo evidence without creating a global inventory ledger.

choices.label: Write the terms plainly
choices.text: Separate quantity, delivery timing, and unresolved points so later checking does not depend on memory.

choices.label: Verify before signing
choices.text: Delay the promise until the record matches what is actually being moved.

events.title: A delivery tests timing rather than a global price formula

variants.text:
An offer looks better than usual, but it arrives too late for a reliable delivery. You compare the extra upside with the risk of missing the window and keep the option to decline without inventing a penalty.

A supplier promises to speed up the next lot, but previous records show several delays. You discuss a concrete date and a backup plan without turning a professional concern into a personal accusation.

The buyer needs part of the order today while the rest can wait. You offer a split delivery only after both sides understand the quantity and timing of each part.

A larger quantity is not always a better deal for the buyer. You first establish how much is actually needed and when, then discuss the delivery without pushing unnecessary volume.

A reliable supplier warns about a possible delay early. Instead of punishing an honest warning, you clarify a backup route and the minimum quantity that can still be delivered.

Before dispatch, you repeat the address, time window, and lot quantity. A simple check takes a minute and reduces the risk of later arguing about what each side thought was obvious.

choices.label: Confirm the delivery window
choices.text: Choose a concrete handoff window and record who is responsible for the next step.

choices.label: Split the delivery
choices.text: Use a narrower delivery commitment to reduce route risk without creating an inventory-capacity system.

events.title: Winter shortage changes the decision, not the global economy

variants.text: When goods are scarce, selling quickly can be tempting, but there is also a cost to breaking commitments already made. You choose between speed and reliability for the specific trade in front of you.

choices.label: Delay the sale
choices.text: Keep the goods and promise narrower timing rather than inventing a universal scarcity multiplier.

choices.label: Reserve a known share for regular buyers
choices.text: Use relationship knowledge rather than a global allocation engine.

choices.label: Accept a narrow high-risk trade
choices.text: Record willingness to carry timing and route risk; this is not a morality or crime label.
